title: Listening: overall strategy
summary: 4 parts, 40 questions, about 30 minutes of audio heard ONCE. Use the reading time to predict answers, and follow the questions in order.
rule: You hear it once: read ahead, follow in order, never stop on a miss.

do: Reading time: limit, key words, predict types
Keep your eyes 1–2 questions ahead
Missed one? Let it go and catch the next
Use pauses to check, then read ahead
avoid: Writing the first thing heard: final version counts
Misspelling a word you know = wrong
Breaking the word limit
remember: Paper: 10 min to transfer; computer: 2 min only
Numbers in digits; no penalty → no blanks

steps: Know the parts: Part 1 everyday conversation (form/note/table: names, numbers, dates). Part 2 monologue (MCQ, map/plan, matching). Part 3 academic discussion (MCQ, matching, choose TWO). Part 4 lecture (note completion, one word per gap).
In the reading time before each part, read the instructions and word limit, underline the key words, and predict each answer type (number? name? plural noun?).
While listening, keep your eyes one or two questions ahead. Answers come in question order.
If you miss an answer, let it go immediately and listen for the next one. Guess at the end.
Use the pause between parts to check the section you finished quickly, then read ahead to the next part.
traps: Stopping on a missed question and losing the next three. Always move forward.
Writing the first thing you hear. Speakers often correct themselves or reject an option. The final version counts.
Spelling: a word you know but misspell is wrong. Illustrative: writing 'accomodation' instead of 'accommodation' scores zero.
Word limit: 'ONE WORD ONLY' + a two-word answer = wrong, even if the meaning is right.
tips: Paper test: 10 minutes at the end to transfer answers. Computer test: only 2 minutes to check, so type the answers as you go.
Write numbers as digits (2020, 429, 19). A number in digits does not count as a word.
Capital letters don't matter, but writing ALL CAPITALS on paper avoids any doubt.
Teacher's ruling: a missing article does not make an answer wrong (key 'a topic / one topic' → 'topic' is accepted). But don't add words that break the limit.
Write the word you heard, not an equivalent: when the key was 'a term', '12 weeks' was marked wrong even though the speaker also said 12 weeks.
Singular/plural: both are accepted only when the key allows it. Check the grammar around the gap ('two ____' → plural).
Never leave a blank: there is no penalty for wrong answers. Rough target: 30/40 ≈ band 7.0, 26 ≈ 6.5, 23 ≈ 6.0.
After the test, read the audioscript for every mistake and write down why (spelling, plural, distractor, word limit, didn't hear).
example: Illustrative: 'My postcode is GT8 2LC — no sorry, it's GT8 2LG.' → write GT82LG. The correction is the answer, copied letter by letter.
language: Corrections: sorry, I mean…; no, wait…; actually…; let me check — oh, it's…; I tell a lie
Rejecting an option: I thought about X, but…; X would be nice, however…; that used to be the case, but now…
Moving on to the next point: right, so…; now, moving on to…; the next thing is…; finally…

title: Form completion
summary: Fill in a form (booking, registration, enquiry) with personal details, numbers and short facts. Mostly Part 1.
rule: Write the final, spelled-out version: speakers often correct themselves.

do: Read the form title and all field labels
Predict each gap: name, number, date, price
Use filled-in fields as landmarks
Check spelling and word limit in the pause
avoid: Similar letters: A/E/I, B/P/V, G/J, M/N
13 vs 30, 15 vs 50; 'double five' = 55
Repeating a unit already printed (£)
remember: Copy codes letter by letter: GT82LC

steps: Read the form title and all the field labels. Imagine the conversation (a booking, a membership, a lost item).
Predict each gap: a name (spelled out), a number, a date, a postcode, a price, a time, a single noun.
Note what is already filled in. The speaker may say it as a landmark just before the next answer.
Write as you listen, then check the spelling and the word limit in the pause.
traps: Letters that sound alike: A/E/I, B/P/V, G/J, M/N, S/F, Q/U. 'Double L' = LL.
Numbers: thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty (-teen is stressed at the end). 'Oh' = 0, 'double five' = 55, 'triple' = three of the same.
Corrections: the caller gives a number or date, then changes it. Write the last version.
Prices and times that changed: 'It was £20, but now it's £18' → 18.
Writing the unit when it is already printed next to the gap (£ ____ → just the number).
tips: Codes and postcodes: copy letter by letter, e.g. GT82LC.
Dates: 12 March or March 12 are both fine.
Practise numbers and letters dictation. The teacher posted numbers & letters practice videos for this.
A missing article doesn't make an answer wrong (teacher's ruling), but obey the word limit.
example: Illustrative: Field 'Surname: ____'. Audio: 'It's Jamieson — J-A-M-I-E-S-O-N.' Write the spelled version, not the version you would guess from the sound.
language: Spelling signals: that's spelled…; double S; with a Y at the end; capital…
Correction signals: sorry, I mean…; no, actually…; it was…, but it's changed to…; not X — Y

title: Note completion
summary: Complete notes with words you hear. This is the most common task: Part 1 details and the whole Part 4 lecture.
rule: Write the exact word you hear; check grammar, plural and spelling.

do: Read the limit (Part 4: usually ONE WORD)
Use the headings to follow the talk
Predict word type and singular / plural
Listen for the words just before the gap
avoid: Missing plural -s after 'many' or 'two'
Writing a synonym, not the word you heard
Waiting on a gap after a new heading starts
remember: Part 4 has no break: read all 10 gaps first

steps: Read the word limit (Part 4 is usually ONE WORD ONLY).
Read the headings in the notes. They tell you the order of the talk and where you are.
For each gap predict the part of speech and form (noun singular/plural, adjective, verb) from the words around it.
Listen for the paraphrase of the words just before the gap. The answer usually comes right after.
When the speaker moves to a new heading and you still have a gap, leave it and go on.
traps: Plural -s: 'many ____' or 'two ____' need a plural. Illustrative: the speaker says 'several metals', so writing 'metal' is wrong.
Spelling of words you know: weather, environment, necessary, government, accommodation.
Writing a synonym or equivalent instead of the word you heard. The answer must be the word in the recording.
The notes paraphrase the speech, so the word before the gap may not be the word you hear.
tips: In Part 4 there is no break in the middle of the lecture. Read all 10 gaps in the preparation time.
Answers are usually nouns, often less common academic words. You don't need to understand them fully, just spell them correctly.
Check that the completed note makes sense grammatically.
example: Illustrative: Note: 'Some species of ____ can survive in poor soil' (ONE WORD). Audio: '…certain types of fungus are able to live where the soil has few nutrients…' species ↔ types → fungus.
language: Lecture signposts: first of all…; let's turn to…; another important factor is…; to sum up…; an example of this is…
Emphasis that marks an answer: what's crucial here is…; the key thing is…; in particular…

title: Table completion
summary: Fill gaps in a table (e.g. options compared by price, location, features). Read the table the way the speaker will move through it.
rule: Follow the table cell by cell as the speaker goes, usually row by row.

do: Read column headings and row labels
Predict types from filled cells in each column
Track the next cell with your pen
Check spelling, plurals and the word limit
avoid: Losing your place: use the row labels
Features of another option, or 'no longer' ones
Repeating units from the column heading
remember: Common in Parts 1–2; answers are short

steps: Read the column headings and row labels. Decide whether the speaker will go row by row (usually) or column by column.
Look at the filled cells in the same column to predict the type of each answer.
Follow the table with your pen as the speaker talks, so you always know which cell is next.
Check spelling, plurals and the word limit.
traps: Losing your place when the speaker moves to the next row. Use the row labels as landmarks.
Distractors: the speaker mentions a feature of a different option, or one that is 'no longer' available.
Units already printed in the column heading (Price (£), Time (mins)) should not be repeated.
tips: Tables are common in Parts 1–2. The answers are short: a number, a name, one or two nouns.
example: Illustrative: Row 'Hotel B', column 'Disadvantage', other rows say 'noisy', 'far from beach'. Audio: '…it's lovely, but the rooms are rather small…' → small rooms / small (check the limit).
language: Contrast signals for disadvantages: but, the only problem is, the downside is, unfortunately
Next-row signals: as for…; moving on to…; the second one…; then there's…

title: Sentence completion
summary: Complete sentences with words from the recording, within the word limit.
rule: Write the exact words you hear, not an equivalent meaning.

do: Underline key words, predict the word type
Listen for a paraphrase of the sentence start
Write the exact word(s) you hear
Check grammar and the word limit
avoid: Wrong form: noun after 'the', verb after 'to'
Equivalents: key 'a term' ≠ '12 weeks'
remember: Answers follow the order of the recording

steps: Read each sentence and underline the key words. Predict the type of word needed.
Expect the recording to paraphrase the start of the sentence. Listen for the meaning, not the same words.
Write the exact word(s) you hear that complete the sentence grammatically.
Check that the completed sentence makes sense and fits the limit.
traps: The word form must fit the sentence: a noun after 'the', a verb after 'to', an adjective after 'very'.
Equivalent amounts are not accepted. Write the words you heard (the '12 weeks' vs 'a term' case).
tips: Answers follow the order of the recording.
example: Illustrative: 'A module takes ____.' Audio (paraphrased): the speaker says a module takes a term and also mentions twelve weeks → a term / one term / term (article optional), not '12 weeks'.
language: Paraphrase signals: in other words; that is to say; which means

title: Summary completion
summary: Complete a short paragraph summarising part of the talk, with your own heard words or options from a box.
rule: With a box, match the meaning: the word you hear is rarely in the box.

do: Check: words from the audio or a box of letters?
Read the whole summary; predict word types
Box: group the options, think of synonyms
Follow line by line as the speaker talks
avoid: Choosing the box word you heard
Options mentioned but rejected or linked elsewhere

steps: Check whether you write words from the recording or choose letters from a box.
Read the whole summary first to get the story, then predict each gap's word type.
Box version: before the audio, group the options by type (nouns, adjectives) and note synonyms of each, because you will hear paraphrases.
Follow the summary line by line as the speaker talks.
traps: Box version: the word you hear is usually NOT the word in the box. Match meaning.
Options mentioned by the speaker but rejected or attached to a different idea.
tips: Usually in Parts 3–4. Answers are in order.
example: Illustrative: Box option 'expensive'. Audio: '…the main drawback is that it costs a great deal…' → expensive.
language: Paraphrase pairs: costs a great deal ↔ expensive; doesn't last long ↔ short-lived; hard to find ↔ rare

title: Flow-chart completion
summary: Complete the stages of a process or procedure (often a research project in Part 3), with words or option letters.
rule: Follow the speakers' final decision on each step, not their first idea.

do: Follow the arrows before the audio
Predict each box: a noun or an action
Listen for sequence words → next stage
avoid: A step suggested, then changed
Steps said out of order ('before that…')
remember: Letter options: cross out used ones; some unused

steps: Follow the arrows and understand the sequence before the audio.
Predict each box: often a noun (a material, a tool) or a verb/action.
Listen for sequence words. They mark when the speaker moves to the next stage.
traps: Two speakers may discuss a step and then change their minds ('Shall we survey first? — No, let's do the interviews first'). Follow the final decision.
Steps mentioned out of order with 'before that…'.
tips: If the options are letters, cross out those you use. Some options are not used.
example: Illustrative: Box: 'Analyse the ____'. Audio: 'Once we've got the questionnaires back, we'll go through the data…' → data (check if 'results' is the word used).
language: Sequence: first, to start with, after that, once, then, the next stage, finally, before that
Change of plan: actually, let's…; no, we'd better…; on second thoughts

title: Short-answer questions
summary: Answer wh-questions with a few words from the recording.
rule: Write only the words that answer the question, within the limit.

do: Read the limit; underline the question word
Predict the answer type
Listen for the paraphrase; write only the answer
avoid: Full sentences or too many words
'Which TWO…' items can be far apart

steps: Read the word limit and underline the question word (what, where, how much, which TWO).
Predict the type of answer from the question word.
Listen for the paraphrase of the question and write only the answer words.
traps: Writing a full sentence or more words than allowed.
A list question ('Which TWO things…?') may have the items far apart in the recording.
tips: Numbers in digits.
example: Illustrative: Q: 'What should visitors bring?' (ONE WORD) Audio: '…it gets cold at night, so do pack a jacket…' → jacket.
language: Advice/obligation signals: make sure you…; don't forget…; you'll need…; it's essential to…

title: Multiple choice (one answer)
summary: Choose A, B or C. Usually all three are mentioned, but only one answers the question.
rule: All options are usually mentioned; choose the one confirmed at the end.

do: Underline stem key words + option differences
Rephrase the options in your head
Listen for the stem's idea; options follow
Mark ✓ / ✗ as each option is mentioned
avoid: The first option you hear (often rejected)
The option with the recording's exact words
Part 3: one suggests, the other disagrees
remember: Missed it? Guess, move to the next stem

steps: Read the stem and underline the key words. Then underline the key DIFFERENCE between the options.
Rephrase the options in your head so you can recognise paraphrases.
Listen for the stem's idea first. The options come after it.
As each option is mentioned, mark ✓ / ✗. Choose the one that is confirmed at the end, not the first one you hear.
traps: All options are usually mentioned. The distractors are mentioned and then rejected ('I thought about…, but…').
The option that repeats the exact words of the recording is often wrong. The answer is a paraphrase.
In Part 3, one speaker suggests something and the other disagrees. The answer is what they AGREE on or what the question's person thinks.
Past vs present: 'it used to be…, but now…'.
tips: If you missed it, make a quick guess and move straight to the next question. The next stem is your landmark.
Listen for who the question is about: 'What does the woman think…?'
example: Illustrative: Q: 'Where will the group meet?' A café B library C station. Audio: 'Let's meet at the café — oh, it's closed on Mondays. The library then.' → B.
language: Rejection: but, however, actually, the trouble is, that's not really…, I'm not sure about that
Agreement (Part 3): exactly, that's a good point, I agree, yes, let's go with that
Correction: sorry, I mean…; no, wait…; or rather…

title: Choose TWO / THREE letters
summary: Choose two or three options from a list (A–E or more). Each correct letter is one mark, and the letters can be in either order.
rule: Tick only the options confirmed by the speakers' final decision.

do: Read exactly which TWO things are asked
Underline option key words; think of synonyms
Listen to the whole section: answers far apart
Mark ✓ / ✗ / ? as each is discussed
avoid: Rejected options, or true for the wrong person
Negatives about wrong options ('won't be a problem')
remember: Always write two letters, even if unsure

steps: Read the question carefully: which TWO things are they asked about (problems? benefits? things the man will do?).
Underline the key word in each option and think of synonyms.
Listen for the whole section. The two answers can be far apart and come in any order.
Mark each option ✓ / ✗ / ? as it is discussed. Confirm with the speakers' final decision.
traps: Most options are mentioned. Distractors are rejected, are true for the wrong person, or answer a different question.
Answers are often expressed negatively for the wrong options ('that won't be a problem').
tips: Letters can go in either box (IN EITHER ORDER in the answer keys).
Each letter is marked separately, so always write two letters even if you are sure of only one.
This is the third most common listening task in the practice tests, mostly in Parts 2–3.
example: Illustrative: 'Which TWO problems did the students have?' Audio: '…finding participants was hard… the software was fine… but we ran out of time…' → participants + time. 'Software' is the distractor.
language: Positive confirmation: the real problem was, what really helped was, the main advantage
Rejection: wasn't an issue, didn't matter, we didn't need to, that turned out to be fine

title: Matching
summary: Match a list of items (people, places, stages) to options (opinions, features, comments). Common in Parts 2–3.
rule: Items come in order; choose what the speaker finally says or agrees with.

do: Note a key word or synonym next to each option
Read the items: they follow the recording
Hear the item name, then match what's said
Check: can options be used more than once?
avoid: The first option mentioned for an item
Waiting for the same words: expect paraphrase
Losing your place: next item name → move on

steps: Read the options (A–H) and write a short key word or synonym next to each.
Read the numbered items. They come in the order of the recording.
Listen for each item's name, then for what is said about it, and choose the option that paraphrases it.
Check the instructions: options can sometimes be used more than once, and there are more options than items.
traps: Several options are mentioned for each item. Choose the one the speaker finally says or agrees with.
Options are paraphrased opinions, so the same words are rarely heard.
Losing your place: if the next item's name comes up, move on.
tips: Keep your options list visible and cross out used ones (unless reuse is allowed).
example: Illustrative: Item 'The museum shop'. Option D 'offers a discount for students'. Audio: '…and if you show your student card at the shop, you'll pay ten per cent less…' → D.
language: Opinion signals: I found it…; what struck me was…; to be honest…; I wasn't impressed with…
Disagreement (Part 3): I'm not sure I agree; really? I thought…; that's true, but…

title: Map labelling
summary: Match places to letters on a map while the speaker gives a tour or directions. Usually Part 2.
rule: Follow the route from the start point; position words decide the letter.

do: Find the start point and the compass
Name the labelled landmarks
Read the list of places (described in order)
Trace the route with your pen as you listen
avoid: Left / right from the page, not the speaker
'Just past' vs 'just before'; 'opposite' vs 'next to'
Landmarks or old locations that aren't answers
remember: Usually Part 2; places in question order

steps: In the reading time, find the starting point (entrance / 'You are here') and the compass (N is usually up).
Name the labelled landmarks. The speaker will use them to locate the answers.
Read the list of places in order. The speaker usually describes them in question order, moving around the map.
Follow the route with your finger or pen as you listen, and turn the map in your head when the speaker turns.
Listen for position phrases more than nouns: just past, opposite, before you get to, on your left.
traps: Left/right depends on the direction the speaker is facing, not on the page. Follow the route.
'Just past' vs 'just before', 'opposite' vs 'next to'. One preposition changes the letter.
Places on the map that are not answers. The speaker may mention them as landmarks only.
Old vs new layouts: 'the café used to be here, but it has moved to…'.
tips: Learn the teacher's map word list until you recognise it instantly (it is also useful for Writing Task 1 maps).
If you miss one place, wait for the next landmark to find your place again.
example: Illustrative: 'As you come in through the main entrance, the reception is on your right, and just past it, opposite the lifts, is the café.' → café = the letter across from the lifts, beyond reception.
language: Compass: north / south / east / west; northeast, northwest, southeast, southwest; the north side of

Position: in the centre of / in the middle of; above / below; inside / outside; next to; alongside; adjoining; adjacent to; behind; between; in front of; opposite / across from; on the corner; on the right-hand / left-hand side; on the same side of the road as
Route: enter via; go straight (ahead); along; turn left / right; leads off; runs alongside; at the junction; dead end; just past; a little beyond; before you get to; upon entering…, it's on the right
Location verbs: is located / situated / positioned; faces; centrally located

title: Plan labelling (floor plan / layout)
summary: Label rooms or areas on a building plan or site layout, usually from a guided tour in Part 2.
rule: Walk in from the entrance with the speaker; place rooms by labelled ones.

do: Find the entrance and the labelled rooms
Decide which way you face as you walk in
Read the room list (described in order)
Listen for positions: between, behind, next to
avoid: Left / right from the page, not the speaker
Rooms that are being moved or planned

steps: Find the entrance and any labelled rooms. Decide which way you 'face' when you walk in.
Read the list of rooms to place. They are described in order.
Follow the speaker through the building: ground floor before upstairs, entrance outwards.
Listen for positions relative to labelled rooms (between the gym and reception, behind the stage).
traps: Left and right from the speaker's position, not from your view of the page.
Rooms that are being moved or planned ('this will be turned into…').
tips: Use the same map vocabulary as for maps. The teacher's examples are building plans: 'the restroom is positioned between the gym and reception', 'the seating area is adjacent to the gym'.
example: Illustrative: 'Go through the entrance, turn left, and the classroom will be straight ahead.' → the room at the end after the left turn from the door.
language: located in front of; faces; situated behind; positioned between; adjacent to; to the left side of; straight ahead; on your left; next to; across from
Floors: on the ground floor, upstairs, downstairs, at the back, at the front, in the far corner

title: Diagram labelling
summary: Label parts of a machine, device or process diagram with words or letters, usually in Parts 3–4.
rule: Use the labelled parts and position words to place each answer.

do: Study the diagram: start point, existing labels
Predict the word type (usually a noun)
Follow the description landmark by landmark
avoid: Catching the noun but ignoring position words
Unknown word? Write what you hear, spell it well

steps: Study the diagram: what is it, and what is labelled already? Find the start of the process or the top of the object.
Predict the word type (usually nouns: a part, a material).
Follow the description in order, using the labelled parts as landmarks and position words as guides.
traps: Position words (above, attached to, underneath) decide which label it is. Don't just catch the noun.
Technical words you don't know: write what you hear and spell carefully.
tips: If the answers are letters from a list, match meaning: the speaker may describe a part's function rather than name it.
example: Illustrative: 'The water collects in a tank at the bottom, and from there a pipe carries it up to the filter.' → the bottom box = tank, the connecting part = pipe.
language: Position/connection: at the top / bottom; underneath; attached to; connected to; inside; surrounding; passes through; flows into
